title: What the River Took
part: PART FOUR: HOLDING UP THE BRIDGE

pages.text:
*From the Bridgewater Almanac: If a thing is afraid, it will hide. If it hides, it must be up to something.*

The water was cold and dark and smelled of silt. Rue waded out, her boots squelching with every step, until she reached the shallow spot where Hobb sat. He looked smaller than usual, his grey-green shoulders hunched, water lapping at his chest. His spectacles were cracked, one lens spiderwebbed with stone dust, and a heavy timber beam was pinned firmly under his arm, holding the nearest arch of the bridge steady against the current.

Rue stopped, her hands trembling on the edge of the stone. Hobb looked up. His eyes were kind, but they were tired in a way she had never seen before.

"Right then," she whispered, her voice thin in the rain. "We are here."

He did not smile. He just nodded, once, slowly. "Fetch rope," he said. His voice was rough, like gravel in a jar. "Thick rope. And then... perhaps a chair."

Cedric stood at the water's edge, his red waistcoat soaked through, his slick hair plastered to his forehead. He was shaking so hard his teeth chattered, a high, thin sound that cut through the drumming of the rain. He stared at the troll, then at Rue, then back at the water, unable to move his feet.
pages.image: A grey-green troll with cracked spectacles sits in a river shallows, pinning a wooden beam under his arm to support a bridge arch, while a small girl in a yellow raincoat wades toward him and a boy in a red waistcoat watches in shock.

pages.text:
The crowd on the bank was silent. It was not the silence of fear, exactly, but of a room where the light is being slowly turned up. People stood in their coats and boots, water dripping from their hems, and they looked at Hobb. They looked at the bridge that had not fallen.

Skye Tanner reached out and took her father’s hand. Her long fair braid was wet and tangled, but her face was steady. She squeezed his fingers once, a small, firm pressure, and then she let go to pull her own coat tighter.

An old man near the front opened his mouth. He started to recite the Almanac, the words coming out in a rush, the usual warnings about hunger and wickedness. But the words died in his throat. He looked at Hobb, who was still holding the beam, still waiting for rope, and the old man closed his mouth. He wiped his face with a sleeve and stepped back, making room for the men with the coils of thick hemp.
pages.image: A quiet crowd of townspeople stands on a muddy riverbank in the rain, watching a troll in the water; a tall girl with a fair braid holds hands with a man, and an old man looks ashamed.

pages.text:
There was no committee. There was no vote. The men of Bridgewater simply moved forward, and the town began to work. They lashed ropes to the arches, bracing the stone against the river’s pull. It was hard, wet, heavy work, and nobody complained.

Gran was at the front. She had brought a dozen kettles, and the steam rose in thick, sweet clouds that smelled of bergamot and sugar. She moved from person to person, pouring tea into cup after cup, her silver bun slightly askew, her flour-dusted sleeves rolled up.

"Sit down, you'll fall down," she told a baker who was leaning on his tools.

"Sit down, you'll fall down," she told the postman, who was staring at the water.

When the ropes were tight and the bridge was secure, Hobb tried to stand. He was too tired. The water was too deep. It took twelve people to help him up the stone steps, each one gripping an arm, a shoulder, or a knee, their faces pale and terrified, but their hands holding on with a strength that surprised even them.
pages.image: A round, silver-haired woman in an apron hands a steaming cup of tea to a tired man on a muddy bank, while a group of villagers helps a large mossy troll climb up stone steps from a river.

pages.text:
Hobb stood, dripping and exhausted, his twine-mended spectacles fogging in the cool air. The crowd parted, not because they wanted to, but because the space around him felt heavy and still.

Cedric stepped out. He was still shaking, his red waistcoat ruined, his hair a mess. He walked into the light of a lantern held by a shopkeeper, and he looked up. The troll’s face was broad and kind, and for a moment Cedric looked very small.

"It was me," Cedric said. His voice cracked. "The first stone. And all the stories. I made them up. I was scared, so I made everybody else scared." He swallowed, his Adam’s apple bobbing. "I don't know how to fix it. I have no way to fix it."

Hobb breathed hard. The sound was like wind in a tunnel. He looked at Cedric for a long time, his eyes sharp behind the cracked glass. Then, very quietly, he said, "Well. You did help me carry the rope."
pages.image: A skinny boy with slicked-back hair and a red waistcoat stands in a lantern's light, looking up at a tall, mossy troll with round spectacles; the troll's expression is serious but not angry, and the boy looks ashamed.

pages.text:
The Mayor pushed forward. He adjusted his top hat, which was damp and bent, and opened his mouth. He was the Mayor. He was the one who made the rules. He was the one who had ordered the Cleansing. He was ready to speak, to explain, to justify.

But the words did not come. He stood there, his mouth open, his face pale, and for the first time in his life, he had nothing to say. He looked at the bridge. He looked at the troll. He looked at Rue, who was watching him with eyes that were dry now, but very hard.

The Mayor slowly took off his top hat. He held it in his hands, a small, dark circle in the grey rain, and he bowed his head.

"Ambrose," Gran said softly. Her voice was not loud, but it carried to everyone. "The toll."

The bell of the old bridge, which no one had rung in three hundred years, rang once. It was a clear, bright sound, shaking the last of the wind from the air, and for a moment, the whole town held its breath.
pages.image: A round, pompous man in a top hat stands with his head bowed and hat in his hands, looking at a group of people including a small girl and a silver-haired woman, while a large stone bridge arch looms behind them in the rain.
